newsitem.title: EGYPT: French minister defends Middle East policy.
newsitem.headline: French minister defends Middle East policy.

text.p: France defended its Middle East policy against Israeli accusations of bias on Monday, saying any settlement must meet Israel's need for security and Arab demands for Israeli withdrawal and Palestinian self-determination.
"The French position is extremely clear. I have called it the middle-of-the road position," French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told reporters in Cairo.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa agreed with him that Europe was well placed to bring about what he called "a balanced peace" between Israel and its neighbours.

De Charette flew to Cairo on Monday, skipping the Israeli leg of a Middle East tour by French President Jacques Chirac because the Israelis refused to let him visit Orient House, the PLO headquarters in Arab East Jerusalem.

Chirac has had a cool reception in Israel because he is advocating a greater European role in Middle East peace talks. He added to the controversy on Monday by telling Israelis that only a Palestinian state could give them security.
De Charette discussed the developments with Arab League Secretary General Esmat Abdel Meguid and later with Moussa.
After the meeting with Abdel Meguid, he said the region was going through a period of crisis.
"The effort of everyone must be to ensure that we can get out of this crisis situation and resume the path of peace. France is making its contribution to that," he said.
Asked how France could convince Israel of its neutrality, de Charette said: "We are very aware of the legitimate preoccupations of both sides.

"For Israel the requirement of security is absolutely essential...In the same way, on the side of the Palestinians, Syrians and Lebanese, questions of territorial integrity, self-determination and development are the central questions."

"The peace process must resume on the basis of accepted principles, U.N. security council resolutions...and the commitments that have been made. All that should make it possible to give both sides the answer to the questions essential to each of them," he added.
De Charette described the French proposal that Europe be joint sponsor of peace talks as "an excellent idea" but declined to say what it would mean in practice.
Moussa, after his meeting with the French minister, said he envisaged Europe as an honest broker in peace talks.

"The European role will be within the framework of honest broker, a helper or a facilitator that appreciates the sensitivies of both parties and that a peace should be balanced and should be equitable. After all it is an Arab-Israeli peace and not an Israeli peace alone," he said.
But de Charette said a European role should not be confrontational or incompatible with the role of the United States, the dominant mediating power.
"I don't think one should present all this in the form of opposition. If one wants peace, one must work hand in hand, one must work in the same direction," he said.

Earlier on Monday Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi told reporters in Cairo that refused to be mere paymaster to the partners in Middle East peace talks and must eventually take on a political role to match its dominant economic presence.
But he added that Europe had no immediate ambitions to mediate directly between Israel and its Arab neighbours.
Prodi, speaking after talks with Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, said it was unrealistic to try to separate political influence and economic contacts.

"Do you think that Europe will be forever the payer and that's all? Do you think this would be realistic -- that we shall go on paying for years and years and increasing our economic presence and just shut up?" he said.
